title: Protocol for Separating Cancer Cell Subpopulations by Metabolic Activity Using Flow Cytometry
author: Blaszczak, White, et al.
materials: NaHCO3-, glucose- and phenol red-free DMEM

steps.title: Prepare loading and sorting media
steps.instruction: Mix the ingredients for lactate‑loading medium, lactate‑free sorting medium, and low‑buffering medium as listed in the Materials; heat each solution to 37 °C, titrate to pH 7.4 with 4 M NaOH or 5 N HCl as needed, sterile‑filter through a 0.22 µm filter, and store at 4 °C until use.

steps.title: Seed cells for assay
steps.instruction: Plate cells at a density that yields at least 18 × 10⁶ cells in 4–7 days (e.g., five 15 cm dishes of MIA PaCa‑2 in RPMI‑1640 with L‑glutamine, NaHCO₃, 10 % FBS, 1 % penicillin‑streptomycin, and 1× sodium pyruvate), replacing medium regularly to avoid acidification.

steps.title: Prepare low‑buffering medium
steps.instruction: Combine the low‑buffering recipe (2 mM HEPES and 2 mM MES, equimolar, adjust NaCl to maintain osmolarity); dissolve, heat to 37 °C, titrate to pH 7.4 (within ±0.05 pH units) with 4 M NaOH or 5 N HCl, sterile‑filter (0.22 µm), and store at 4 °C.

steps.title: Prepare high‑buffering calibration media
steps.instruction: Mix the high‑buffering recipe, divide the solution into 8–10 beakers, heat each to 37 °C and titrate to the desired pH values spanning approximately pH 5 to pH 9 (including one at pH 7.4) with 4 M NaOH or 5 N HCl, record each final pH to three decimal places, sterile‑filter (0.22 µm), and store at 4 °C.

steps.title: Make fluorescent dye stocks
steps.instruction: Dissolve RuBPY in sterile ddH₂O to a 100 mM stock and HPTS in sterile ddH₂O to a 4 mM stock; mix the two stocks 1:1 (v/v) to generate the working dye mixture, protect from light, and store aliquots at –20 °C for up to 2 months.

steps.title: Calibrate pH‑ and O₂‑sensitive dyes
steps.instruction: Under sterile conditions thaw the RuBPY/HPTS mixture, dilute 1:1000 (v/v) in high‑buffering medium, load 100 µL per well of a black‑wall/clear‑bottom 96‑well plate (triplicates per point), place the plate in a 37 °C microplate reader with a CO₂‑free, dual‑gas controller, set O₂ to 21 % and record fluorescence until stable (F1: 510 nm/400 nm, F2: 510 nm/460 nm, F3: 510 nm/416 nm, F4: 620 nm/450 nm), repeat at O₂ levels 15 %, 10 %, 5 %, 2.5 %, and 1 % (same pH points), export data and compute RpH = F2/F1 (at 21 % O₂) and RO₂ = F3/F4 (at pH 7.4), fit the pH calibration curve pH = pKa − log((rmax − RpH)/(RpH − rmin)) and the O₂ calibration line RO₂ = a − b·exp(−PO₂·t) (normalize to 21 % O₂, with typical ranoxia ≈ 0.7).

steps.title: Determine oil barrier O₂ permeability
steps.instruction: Load a 96‑well plate with 100 µL of the dye‑containing high‑buffering medium at pH 7.4, gently add light mineral oil to achieve volumes of 0, 50, 100, and 150 µL per well (touch pipette tip to wall), incubate the plate at 37 °C in a CO₂‑free, minimal‑O₂ atmosphere for ≥6 h to deplete O₂, quickly transfer the lid‑less plate to the microplate reader set to 37 °C, CO₂‑free, 21 % O₂, and record F3 and F4 at 1–5 min intervals until a plateau is reached; export the data, calculate RO₂ = F3/F4 over time, and fit a mono‑exponential curve RO₂ = a − b·exp(−PO₂·t) to obtain the oil permeability PO₂, which will be used to correct cellular O₂ consumption measurements.

steps.title: Run metabolic analysis script
steps.instruction: In RStudio open analysis_script.Rmd, load the exported plate‑reader workbook formatted like example_workbook.xlsx, update the calibration variables and setup‑specific constants, execute the script, and obtain Excel output files summarizing medium pH, cumulative acid production (µmol), medium O₂ (%), and cumulative O₂ consumption (µmol) for each time interval and sorted subpopulation.

description: A key phenotype of cancer cells is their metabolic activity, which includes a description of lactic acid fermentation and mitochondrial respiration that supply energy and building blocks for proliferation. Metabolic activity is determined by the abundance, distribution, and activity of enzymes and transporters, as well as the spatio-temporal profile of substrates, intermediates, and products. This complexity provides scope for dynamic metabolic heterogeneity which manifests in cancers, ostensibly because it may offer a growth advantage. However, mechanisms of this heterogeneity are challenging to study because metabolic rate is difficult to resolve at single-cell level, let alone use it to separate sub-populations by metabolic phenotype. Single-cell transcriptomics and proteomics can describe the network of enzymes and transporters, but fluxes are not readily inferred from this information. Single-cell metabolomics provide a snapshot of metabolite abundance at steady-state, rather than their flux. Attempts to separate cells by metabolic activity should consider a metric related to flux that can be implemented for sorting techniques, such as FACS. Fluorescent sensors of metabolite abundance are now available for real-time measurements, but sorting by these signals separates cells by steady-state metabolite levels, which is not necessarily proportional to flux. The challenge is that conventional flow cytometry takes a single measurement per cell, which – by definition – cannot interrogate changes over time. One strategy could involve a carefully timed experiment, where a substrate is added and its intracellular abundance probed flow-cytometrically after a fixed time delay. However, this may require cells to be substrate-depleted to assign a baseline: a maneuver that may affect metabolism.
